item.title: My Samsung Galaxy phone battery finally lasted all day after I changed one setting
item.itunes:title: My Samsung Galaxy phone battery finally lasted all day after I changed one setting
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My Galaxy S25 Ultra’s battery life wasn’t terrible, but it had one annoying problem: it almost never made it comfortably through the entire day. By evening, I was already looking for a charger. I had tried the usual power-saving mode and other tricks, but most of them either made little difference or came with compromises I didn’t want (like suspending notifications).

Eventually, I changed one harmless setting that I had been using for months. And the difference was enough to change how I use my phone throughout the day.

6 features I immediately disable on my Google Pixel

Even Google's clean take on Android needs a bit of tweaking.

3
By  Patrick O'Rourke

I never suspected Always On Display first

Then I checked the Battery menu

Whenever my Galaxy S25 Ultra struggled to make it through the day, Always On Display was never the first thing I blamed. After all, I never wanted to touch my perfect One UI setup in the first place. My instinct was to look at the usual power-saving options instead.

I considered turning on power-saving mode more often, restricting background apps, and tweaking performance settings. But before changing anything that could affect how I actually use the phone, I opened the Battery section in Settings to see where the power was really going.

That is when Always On Display caught my attention. It consistently accounted for about 8-10% of my battery usage, which was far more than I expected from something as simple as showing a clock and notifications.

I limit charging on my Galaxy S25 Ultra to 90% for better battery longevity. And by the time my phone is down to 5%, a consumption of around 10% just from Always On Display is quite huge.

At the time, I was getting only around four hours of screen-on time, and by evening, I was already reaching for a charger. Instead of compromising the entire phone with Power Saving mode, I decided to deal with the obvious culprit first.

I tweaked the AOD setting

From Scheduled to Tap to show

Samsung, being Samsung, has no shortage of customization options, and Always On Display is no exception. I can keep it on all the time, show it only for new notifications, schedule it for specific hours, or make it appear only when I tap the screen.

Earlier, I had mine scheduled from 10 AM to 2 AM, which meant it was active for almost my entire working day. At the time, that felt like the most convenient setup.

Instead of turning it off entirely, I have now switched it to Tap to show (from Settings -> Lock screen and AOD -> Always On Display -> When to show menu), and surprisingly, I don’t feel like I have given up much at all. Whenever I want to check time, notifications, calendar information, or supported widgets, I simply tap the screen once, and everything appears instantly.

It still gives me the same quick-glance experience, just without keeping AOD active for hours when I am not even looking at the phone.

More importantly, I didn’t have to change anything else to see the benefit. I didn’t enable the Power Saving mode, lower the refresh rate, turn off 5G, restrict apps aggressively, or compromise performance. My S25 Ultra still behaves exactly the way I want it to. I simply changed how AOD works, and that alone was enough to improve my daily battery endurance.

I turned my Samsung Galaxy into a speed machine by ditching Samsung's bloated launcher

The official launcher is of no good.

1
By  Anurag Singh

I didn’t really lose the convenience

And got back my full-day battery

I didn’t really lose the convenience of Always On Display. It is still there whenever I need it. A single tap on the screen brings up the time, notifications, calendar information, and widgets, so the experience still feels familiar.

The battery results have been much more noticeable than I expected. Earlier, Always On Display regularly appeared in the Battery menu with a major share of my daily usage. After switching to Tap to show, it no longer shows up there as a battery drain.

That alone tells me the change is doing exactly what I wanted. More importantly, the screen-on time has improved from around four hours to more than five hours on many days.

An extra hour may not sound dramatic on paper, but in daily use, it has made a huge difference. That extra buffer is often the difference between reaching for a charger in the evening and simply making it through the day.

My phone charger finally stays at home

I still like Samsung’s Always On Display, but I no longer think it needs to stay visible for most of the day. Switching to Tap to show gave me the best of both worlds. I can still check everything whenever I want, but I am no longer watching battery, keeping that information on-screen constantly.

That simple change finally pushed my screen-on time past five hours and gave me the battery fix in no time.

If your Samsung phone feels slow, disable these features to make it better.

item.title: I tried this open-source platform to self-host LLMs, and it’s faster than I expected
item.itunes:title: I tried this open-source platform to self-host LLMs, and it’s faster than I expected
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My AI world was limited to the big names like ChatGPT and Gemini. A few months back, I started exploring the world of self-hosted LLMs. I started using multiple self-hosted LLMs for different tasks. My experiments with self-hosted LLMs were primarily limited to Ollama and LM Studio. While both are excellent tools, I always wanted something that perfectly balanced an easy setup with deep customization. That's when I discovered Koboldcpp, and it completely changed my perspective. I set up Koboldcpp on my laptop, which is equipped with an Intel Core Ultra 9 processor, 32GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4050 GPU. Not only was the setup incredibly simple, but the performance was so much faster than I ever thought possible.

What is Koboldcpp?

Installation is a breeze

Koboldcpp is an all-in-one software that enables you to run large language models (LLMs) directly on your own PC. It's built on the llama.cpp project, which makes it well-optimized for both CPU and GPU. With a customizable web interface featuring multiple themes, Koboldcpp allows you to easily manage persistent stories, characters, and even integrate image, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech features.

The platform bundles everything you need into a single, straightforward executable. Honestly, I was expecting a complicated process involving command lines and compiling, but the installation was a complete breeze. I just went to their GitHub page and downloaded a single .exe file. No messy dependencies, no multi-step wizard; just one file to download. I ran it, and a small settings window popped up. In just a few minutes, I was ready to load my first model.

The key to getting started is finding the right model file. Koboldcpp primarily works with GGML and the newer models. The recommended model type is GGUF. They are easily available on HuggingFace. I simply searched for "GGUF" along with the model, which was Meta-Llma-3.1.

Once I had downloaded a model file, using it was incredibly easy. From the Koboldcpp startup window, I just clicked "Browse," found my .gguf file, selected it, and hit "Start." The web interface loaded instantly, opening a clean and customizable environment. It even has different themes, so I could make it feel just right. From there, I could just start typing.

The whole process, from finding the model to generating my first text, took less time than I spent brewing my morning coffee.

I can play with texts, images, and audio

It is faster than I expected

The most exciting part of using Koboldcpp for me was realizing it's so much more than a simple text generator. After I got my text model running and was happily creating stories, I discovered it could do a lot more. I could even do image generation with models like Stable Diffusion. With the suitable model files, I was able to create pictures directly from my text prompts. I also experimented with its audio features. By loading a Whisper model for speech-to-text, I could talk into my mic and have my words instantly typed out. For an even better experience, I used a text-to-speech model to have the AI "read" its answers back to me. All of this happens locally, without any internet connection.

My earlier attempts at running LLMs on my own computer were a bit slow. I'd wait for the model to process my prompts, which felt more like a chore than a conversation. That's why I felt pretty impressed with Koboldcpp. The moment I hit "Generate," the words just started appearing on the screen. The speed was incredible. It completely changed my mind about what’s possible with a local LLM setup.

It has many interesting power user features

Packed with features, built for everyone

What I appreciate most about Koboldcpp is that it's designed for everyone, from beginners to power users. Beyond the simple setup, it's packed with advanced features. It has a ton of customization options. I can fine-tune things like repetition penalty, temperature, and Top-P to control how the AI generates text, making it more creative or more focused. This level of control is something you just don't get with online platforms.

Another huge benefit is its broad hardware support. It works with various GPUs, including NVIDIA and AMD. It means you can achieve great performance regardless of the type of graphics card you have. When I load a model, I can specify how many "GPU layers" I want to offload. This allows me to utilize my GPU's VRAM efficiently, striking a perfect balance between speed and memory usage. It’s also built to be used with other front-ends like SillyTavern, which opens up a new world of customization and role-playing features. This flexibility and user-friendly interface for managing advanced settings really make it stand out.

Is it better than competitors?

Having tried platforms like Ollama and LM Studio, I can say that Koboldcpp stands out for its unique blend of simplicity and power. While Ollama is great for a command-line approach and LM Studio has a polished all-in-one GUI, Koboldcpp feels like it hits the sweet spot. It features an easy, single-file setup and a user-friendly interface, but it doesn't compromise the deep customization that power users require.

Of course, it’s not perfect. It primarily works with limited model types, so you can't just use any model file you download from Hugging Face, unlike other tools. This means you'll have to make sure you're downloading a compatible file, which can be a minor extra step. However, for a user who wants full control over the local AI and appreciates the ability to fine-tune every little setting for the fastest possible performance, Koboldcpp is worth trying. Despite any minor limitations, its speed and flexibility make it a useful tool for anyone interested in self-hosting LLMs.

Koboldcpp

item.title: Old GPUs are finally practical for home server AI, and you don't need 24GB of VRAM to replace cloud models
item.itunes:title: Old GPUs are finally practical for home server AI, and you don't need 24GB of VRAM to replace cloud models
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Although the LLMs on ChatGPT, Perplexicity, and other cloud-based AI platforms have terrific reasoning capabilities, locally-hosted models have some major perks up their sleeve. Since they run on local hardware, you don’t need to spend extra bucks every month or deal with rate limits to run multiple inference jobs in a short amount of time. Likewise, local LLMs are significantly better for productivity tasks centered around financial records, academic details, personal projects, and confidential files, as they respect your privacy instead of storing data on some random company’s cloud.

The drawback, of course, is that you need a lot of processing prowess to drive models that don’t devolve into a hallucinating mess… Or, at least, that’s how it used to be when local LLMs started making the rounds. These days, it’s entirely possible to get powerful LLMs up and running on consumer-tier graphics cards at respectable speeds.

Two old GPUs I salvaged are doing more AI work than a brand new $2000 card, and I won't be upgrading anytime soon

I built a local AI setup out of two old GPUs that sell for cheap, and it beats a single new card

3
By  Ayush Pande

item.title: My old laptop plays my desktop's games now, and the whole setup took one evening
item.itunes:title: My old laptop plays my desktop's games now, and the whole setup took one evening
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As someone who grew up with a laptop, I'm painfully familiar with the compromises one has to expect when they try to "game" on this form-factor. Thin and light machines usually don't have enough GPU horsepower to run modern AAA games, and after a certain point, no amount of dropping settings can change the hardware ceiling. Even the machines that can brute-force their way through demanding titles eventually run into the other problem, which is heat.

Then, of course, there's the software side of problems. If you're on macOS like me, hardware limitations are only the beginning of the issue. A huge chunk of the PC gaming library simply isn't available. For many years, I just accepted all of this as a cost of portability. But then one evening, I pointed Moonlight at my desktop, and every single one of those problems became my desktop's job.

The trick was to move the graphical heavy-lifting elsewhere

My M2 Air only needs to decode a video, not render a game

The problem with gaming on a laptop is primarily the fact that it has to have the right chip combination, and a thermal design that's enough to support it. A CPU to feed it, a GPU to render it, and cooling that can keep both from cooking themselves, or your lap, if that's how you use your device. On top of that, it needs a battery that's big enough to survive the ordeal. My fanless M2 MacBook Air has none of that, but even then, I can game on it just as well as I can on my desktop.

With Sunshine running on my desktop, the RTX 4070 Ti Super with 16GB of GDDR6X does all the graphical grunt work. It handles the game, handles ray-tracing, applies whatever obnoxiously high setting I throw at it, and hands the finished frames to its NVENC encoder, while the MacBook never renders a polygon. It receives a video stream and displays it, and that's literally all it needs to do here.

Moonlight and Apollo help me experience my PC games the console way

My PlayStation is shaking in terror

By  Samarveer Singh

Sunshine and Moonlight are the only two apps I need

A quick install later, I don't have to be "on my desk" to play

Sunshine and Moonlight are the only two apps I need, and both are completely free and open-source. Sunshine goes on the host, which is my desktop, and Moonlight goes on Mac, which is also available on App Store. It's easy to get confused between the two, so I think of it this way: the Sun casts light upon the moon and the moon reflects the sunlight, so Sunshine goes on the host, while Moonlight goes on the client. It's silly, but it helps me to remember.

The most beautiful aspect of this setup is that my Mac's gaming performance is completely irrelevant. Whether my GPU is rendering a game using DLSS 4.5, ray tracing, or deploying smooth motion, the M2 sees none of the overhead and does the same job of decoding the incoming video stream and putting those frames on its display. Because I have a decent GPU, it virtually guarantees that most of my games hit the 60Hz refresh rate ceiling on my laptop before throughput ever becomes a problem.

Obviously, the workload is easier than rendering a modern game on the device, going through compatibility requirements (or working around them), downloading it on my laptop, and running it at whatever graphical preset the device allows. The M2 has dedicated media hardware for decoding formats like HEVC, so Moonlight isn't relying on the CPU to painstakingly chew through every frame.

4 reasons why a Sunshine + Moonlight setup is better than Parsec

While it's not the best option for remote desktop setups, a Sunshine and Moonlight combo is perfect for gamers

1
By  Ayush Pande

Any modern gaming PC can be the host

You don't need a cutting-edge GeForce RTX to pull this off

While I use a 40-series GPU in my streaming setup, it's possible to basically use any Nvidia or AMD GPU which has a hardware video encoder. That covers NVENC on anything from GTX 900 series onwards, AMD's VCN encoder on Radeon cards, and even Intel's QuickSync if you're using an Arc GPU. If your desktop can run the game, you can almost certainly stream it too, and it doesn't eat into performance at all because encoding happens on a dedicated block.

For the decoding, literally every modern device works, from an iPhone (which I tested it on) to a gaming handheld like the Steam Deck or the Lenovo Legion Go. That's because Moonlight's floor is hardware H.264 decode, which every phone, tablet, laptop, and streaming box from the last decade has.

The parts of this setup that I expected to struggle with are the ones that surprised me the most. I paired my Xbox One Elite 2 controller to the Mac, and Sunshine simply presented it to my desktop as a virtual gamepad. There was no need for additional driver installation or lengthy configuration that would take up my time.

Audio was just as effortless, because Sunshine captures my PC's output and sends it alongside the video. The latency was perhaps the most impressive aspect of it all, mostly because I would regularly forget that the game wasn't even running locally.

Sunshine

Sunshine is a free, open-source app that lets any gaming PC broadcast itself that any Moonlight client can connect to.

See at Github

Sunshine and Moonlight changed how and where I game, and I couldn't be more grateful

I've probably said it before, but I will say it every single time I mention the Sunshine/Moonlight combo. I strongly believe that anyone with a gaming PC who doesn't know about it yet, is categorically missing out on a great gaming experience. I don't throw around the word "revolutionary" often, but right now, I can't think of a better way to describe what the duo does to gaming.

As someone with a gaming PC, I obviously love gaming, but I don't want to be sat at my desk right next to my roaring rig and be exposed to the heat it generates in the middle of a summer afternoon when I'm just trying to casually grind levels through Digimon Story: Time Stranger. The open source software ecosystem has given me an option to leave the desk behind, jump on my bed, lie down at whichever awkward angle I want, and continue playing on a fanless M2 Macbook Air.

Thin and light machines usually don't have enough GPU horsepower to run modern AAA games, and after a certain point, no amount of dropping settings can change the hardware ceiling. Even the machines that can brute-force their way through demanding titles eventually run into the other problem, which is heat.

Then, of course, there's the software side of problems. If you're on macOS like me, hardware limitations are only the beginning of the issue. A huge chunk of the PC gaming library simply isn't available. For many years, I just accepted all of this as a cost of portability. But then one evening, I pointed Moonlight at my desktop, and every single one of those problems became my desktop's job.

The trick was to move the graphical heavy-lifting elsewhere

My M2 Air only needs to decode a video, not render a game

The problem with gaming on a laptop is primarily the fact that it has to have the right chip combination, and a thermal design that's enough to support it. A CPU to feed it, a GPU to render it, and cooling that can keep both from cooking themselves, or your lap, if that's how you use your device. On top of that, it needs a battery that's big enough to survive the ordeal. My fanless M2 MacBook Air has none of that, but even then, I can game on it just as well as I can on my desktop.

With Sunshine running on my desktop, the RTX 4070 Ti Super with 16GB of GDDR6X does all the graphical grunt work. It handles the game, handles ray-tracing, applies whatever obnoxiously high setting I throw at it, and hands the finished frames to its NVENC encoder, while the MacBook never renders a polygon. It receives a video stream and displays it, and that's literally all it needs to do here.

Moonlight and Apollo help me experience my PC games the console way

My PlayStation is shaking in terror

By  Samarveer Singh

Sunshine and Moonlight are the only two apps I need

A quick install later, I don't have to be "on my desk" to play

Sunshine and Moonlight are the only two apps I need, and both are completely free and open-source. Sunshine goes on the host, which is my desktop, and Moonlight goes on Mac, which is also available on App Store. It's easy to get confused between the two, so I think of it this way: the Sun casts light upon the moon and the moon reflects the sunlight, so Sunshine goes on the host, while Moonlight goes on the client. It's silly, but it helps me to remember.

The most beautiful aspect of this setup is that my Mac's gaming performance is completely irrelevant. Whether my GPU is rendering a game using DLSS 4.5, ray tracing, or deploying smooth motion, the M2 sees none of the overhead and does the same job of decoding the incoming video stream and putting those frames on its display. Because I have a decent GPU, it virtually guarantees that most of my games hit the 60Hz refresh rate ceiling on my laptop before throughput ever becomes a problem.

Obviously, the workload is easier than rendering a modern game on the device, going through compatibility requirements (or working around them), downloading it on my laptop, and running it at whatever graphical preset the device allows. The M2 has dedicated media hardware for decoding formats like HEVC, so Moonlight isn't relying on the CPU to painstakingly chew through every frame.

4 reasons why a Sunshine + Moonlight setup is better than Parsec

While it's not the best option for remote desktop setups, a Sunshine and Moonlight combo is perfect for gamers

1
By  Ayush Pande

Any modern gaming PC can be the host

You don't need a cutting-edge GeForce RTX to pull this off

While I use a 40-series GPU in my streaming setup, it's possible to basically use any Nvidia or AMD GPU which has a hardware video encoder. That covers NVENC on anything from GTX 900 series onwards, AMD's VCN encoder on Radeon cards, and even Intel's QuickSync if you're using an Arc GPU. If your desktop can run the game, you can almost certainly stream it too, and it doesn't eat into performance at all because encoding happens on a dedicated block.

For the decoding, literally every modern device works, from an iPhone (which I tested it on) to a gaming handheld like the Steam Deck or the Lenovo Legion Go. That's because Moonlight's floor is hardware H.264 decode, which every phone, tablet, laptop, and streaming box from the last decade has.

The parts of this setup that I expected to struggle with are the ones that surprised me the most. I paired my Xbox One Elite 2 controller to the Mac, and Sunshine simply presented it to my desktop as a virtual gamepad. There was no need for additional driver installation or lengthy configuration that would take up my time.

Audio was just as effortless, because Sunshine captures my PC's output and sends it alongside the video. The latency was perhaps the most impressive aspect of it all, mostly because I would regularly forget that the game wasn't even running locally.

Sunshine

Sunshine is a free, open-source app that lets any gaming PC broadcast itself that any Moonlight client can connect to.

See at Github

Sunshine and Moonlight changed how and where I game, and I couldn't be more grateful

I've probably said it before, but I will say it every single time I mention the Sunshine/Moonlight combo. I strongly believe that anyone with a gaming PC who doesn't know about it yet, is categorically missing out on a great gaming experience. I don't throw around the word "revolutionary" often, but right now, I can't think of a better way to describe what the duo does to gaming.

As someone with a gaming PC, I obviously love gaming, but I don't want to be sat at my desk right next to my roaring rig and be exposed to the heat it generates in the middle of a summer afternoon when I'm just trying to casually grind levels through Digimon Story: Time Stranger. The open source software ecosystem has given me an option to leave the desk behind, jump on my bed, lie down at whichever awkward angle I want, and continue playing on a fanless M2 Macbook Air.

item.title: 6 open-source Windows tools saved me over $400 a year
item.itunes:title: 6 open-source Windows tools saved me over $400 a year
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I used to think good Windows software always came with a price tag, especially when I needed something beyond the basics. Over time, though, I started testing open-source apps and found myself questioning several software purchases I had made. Some were surprisingly polished, while others simply did their job without getting in my way. That changed how I choose software. Instead of reaching for a paid app whenever I need a new tool, I now check what the open-source community has built first.

Everything

The fastest way I find files

The first app that made me question why I was still paying for software was Everything. I used to waste more time than I realized looking for files on my Windows PC. Windows Search often felt slower than I wanted, especially when I knew exactly what I was looking for but couldn't remember where I'd saved it.

Everything changed that for me. I can start typing a filename and get the result almost instantly. I also like that it stays focused on one job instead of trying to become a complete file-management suite. Once I got used to relying on it, searching for files became a quick habit rather than a small chore. It's a simple utility, but it has saved me enough time to make it one of those apps I keep installed.

Ditto

The clipboard feature Windows was missing

Ditto solved another small Windows problem that I didn't realize was costing me time: copying and pasting the same things repeatedly. I often need to move several pieces of text between apps, and the standard Windows clipboard only keeps track of so much. With Ditto, I can go back through my clipboard history and pick something I copied earlier instead of copying it again.

I find this especially useful when I'm working on long articles and moving notes, links, quotes, or bits of text around. It quietly sits in the background and becomes useful whenever I need it. I don't have to change how I work either. I just press the shortcut, find the item I want, and paste it. For me, that made the clipboard far more useful.

GIMP

Say goodbye to costly Photoshop

GIMP is the app that stopped me from feeling like I needed Photoshop for every image-related task. As a blogger, I regularly need to prepare images before they go into an article, and I don't need a huge collection of professional design tools to do that. GIMP gives me enough control to work comfortably with images without paying for a monthly plan.

I can make the changes I need, save the finished file, and move on with my work. What I appreciate most is that it doesn't lock basic editing behind a subscription. It took me a little time to get comfortable with the interface, but once I learned where the tools were, it stopped feeling complicated. For my everyday image work, GIMP has been more than enough.

SumatraPDF

Why pay for Adobe Acrobat?

SumatraPDF replaced another piece of software I had little reason to keep paying for. I mainly need a PDF reader for opening documents, checking pages, and quickly referring to files while working. I don't need a full suite of editing tools every time I open a PDF, and SumatraPDF keeps things simple. It launches quickly and doesn't make me wait through a heavy interface before I can read a document.

I also like how uncluttered it feels compared with some of the larger PDF applications I've used. No unnecessary features get in the way when all I want to do is read something. For my everyday PDF needs, that focused approach works well. It feels like the kind of lightweight Windows utility that should have been included from the start.

17
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

LocalSend

Moving files finally became painless

LocalSend saved me from relying on paid file-transfer services whenever I needed to move something between my devices. As a blogger, I regularly work across my PC and phone, and sending a file to myself felt unnecessarily awkward. LocalSend gave me a much simpler way to handle those moments.

I can transfer photos, documents, screenshots, and other files directly between devices on the same network. There is no need to create an account or upload something to a third-party service just to get it onto another device. That makes it particularly handy when I need to move a file quickly and don't want to think about storage limits or subscription plans. It has become one of those small utilities I appreciate more the longer I use it.

ShareX

A screenshot tool that does everything

Taking screenshots is something I do almost every day while researching and writing, so I wanted a tool that could keep up without adding another subscription to my expenses. ShareX turned out to be exactly what I needed. I can quickly capture a selected area, a window, or the entire screen depending on what I'm working on. I also like being able to assign shortcuts to the actions I use most, which saves me from reaching for menus every time.

There are plenty of options for handling a capture after I take it, so I can fit the process around my workflow rather than changing how I work. I don't need a separate paid screenshot utility anymore. For something I use so frequently, having all these features available without a subscription has made a noticeable difference.

6 software subscriptions I cancelled after finding free alternatives

I saved hundreds by cancelling these software subscriptions

29
By  Parth Shah

I’m done paying for software I barely need

I’m not against paid software, but I’ve realized I don’t need a subscription for every task on my PC. These open-source apps have covered enough of my everyday workflow that paying for expensive alternatives often feels unnecessary. The bigger lesson for me is simple: before buying another piece of software, I now look for an open-source option first. Sometimes, the free tool is all I actually need.

item.title: I finally stopped paying monthly security fees thanks to this lightweight, self-hosted NVR
item.itunes:title: I finally stopped paying monthly security fees thanks to this lightweight, self-hosted NVR
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've got a number of UniFi cameras around my home. While the cameras themselves are plenty good, recording with them comes with a bit of a problem. UniFi's entire camera ecosystem is designed around using its own NVR and software. While the software works fine enough on my DreamMachine Pro, I've been looking to offload that to a dedicated server.

But I didn't want another appliance to store camera footage. So, I started looking for NVR software to deploy on my existing server. Something that could take the RTSP stream from my UniFi cameras and record it locally. It'd give me the useful parts of the security system without having me locked into yet another piece of hardware. That's where VibeNVR steps in. It takes the RTSP streams from my cameras and feeds them into proper NVR software complete with recordings, motion detection, event history, and more.

I paired a local LLM with Frigate and Home Assistant, and my smart cameras finally understand what they are looking at

My smart home camera alerts used to be useless, but now they tell me what actually happened

3
By  Ayush Pande

VibeNVR gets the important NVR features right

Smarter streaming and easier footage reviewing

Credit: 

The biggest appeal of this Docker-based app is that it fits in my existing setup seamlessly. Once the cameras are configured to provide their RTSP feeds, VibeNVR immediately picks up from there. I get a live view of the cameras through the web interface, with recordings being stored locally. It might sound basic, but it is exactly what I'm looking for in an NVR.

Using a software-based NVR also lets me decide how much storage I want to allocate. VibeNVR uses a storage quota-based system so I can set a fixed amount of storage after which it automatically purges older footage and records fresh footage. Video recording can eat through storage astonishingly quickly, so a system with automatic retention controls and storage limits is essential, not really an option.

Moreover, this is handy because I don't personally need weeks of footage sitting on my system. A couple of days is more than enough. If something goes wrong, I know, and I need to be able to scrub through the last 24-48 hours. Of course, your circumstances might be different, and a system such as this gives you flexibility to opt for whatever works for you.

Elsewhere, I like that VibeNVR supports multiple storage locations and even tiered storage. This means you can effectively set up a dual-drive archival system of sorts. Since I don't need that, I haven't set it up, but features like these help sell the system as a properly thought-out NVR alternative.

VibeNVR has all the features I need

Finding the right footage takes seconds

The depth of features here is quite exhaustive, making it impossible to touch every facet. However, some of the other features that have stood out to me include the ability to maintain separate streams for different jobs. Since my live view feed has multiple cameras streaming to it, I've set up a low-resolution RTSP stream to keep things efficient. Meanwhile, a high-resolution stream is set up for recording.

Elsewhere, an NVR is only as easy as it makes it to review footage. That's where VibeNVR gets particularly interesting. It can detect motion and create events around activities. It even allows me to get straight to the footage instead of manually scrubbing through an entire recording.

It certainly helps that the app has taken a lot of inspiration from UniFi's interface. But that's fine; the interface is great, easy to use, and more importantly, easy to help you get to your footage.

VibeNVR's event timeline gives me a great way to approach the problem of hours of static footage. I can go back to a particular time within seconds. Once configured, you'll also find object detection support that can identify and flag elements like people, vehicles, and animals. This, in my opinion, is an equally important part of a competent NVR, and VibeNVR does it extremely well.

Motion zones are useful for the same purpose. My camera on my balcony overlaps the road in front of it, and I do not want to get motion triggers for random cars passing down the street. By restricting detection to the areas that matter, I can cut down on the noise and make the event history more useful. Building on that same feature, the privacy mask feature lets you block out sections of the image. For example, the same camera looks into a window as well, and a privacy mask blocks that section of the image out.

All that to say is that the app has basically all NVR functions you could need, including the ability to control PTZ cameras.

VibeNVR fits completely into my existing server setup

Spinning up VibeNVR has been a fantastic addition to my server, as it's let me add my camera recordings to my existing setup. It gives you local recordings, an easy way to find events, and flexibility to decide where the footage lives. And that's basically what I wanted from the start. Not another appliance or piece of hardware, but just a simple way to get more control over my security cameras and recordings.

item.title: Please don't expose your new NAS to the internet
item.itunes:title: Please don't expose your new NAS to the internet
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Setting up a NAS takes a lot of weight off your PC's shoulders and reduces the financial strain of cloud storage and streaming services, too. They are often marketed as your personal, private cloud with oodles of expandable storage and redundancy protection for your backups, media, and important files, all accessible from any device on your Wi-Fi. On your local home network, it's a secure, fast, and convenient data vault that can run several self-hosted services as well.

However, extending that personal cloud beyond your four walls to access your files from a hotel, or automatically back up your phone's photos while you're on vacation, is deceptively simple. When starting out with a new NAS, you could easily flick a few switches in your router settings to make your NAS visible to the public internet. Inadvertently or otherwise, this is a dangerous proposition because what enables remote access for you may also make your NAS and home network a glowing beacon for cyberattackers. Without setting up secure tunnels or a VPN, you're jeopardizing multiple devices and your digital existence. Allow me to explain.

The cloud replacement myth

Marketing isn't always the whole truth

A NAS is frequently marketed as the ultimate cloud storage replacement, but that's only half the story. Yes, it replaces the storage part, but it doesn't automatically replace the robust, professionally managed security and accessibility of a cloud enterprise operating at scale. Without an off-site backup for your NAS on separate, offline drives, you're one disaster away from losing everything. Sure, a RAID configuration offers reassurance against drive failure within the NAS, but backups ensure you're insulated from natural calamities or ransomware attacks wiping out your NAS. For this reason alone, if you're a new NAS owner, you should strongly consider using it exclusively on your home network at first. Taking your NAS online can quickly prove to be a big mistake.

Exposing your NAS to the internet typically happens if you set up port forwarding on your router to allow traffic from the outside world to access storage and other devices on your home network. Synology's setup process for a new NAS famously offers this as an option through the QuickConnect service. If you use the default settings and forward the default ports (like 5000/5001 for Synology or 8080/443 for QNAP), you are essentially painting a massive target on your back. You're telling every automated port scanner bot and malicious actor on the internet about your consumer-grade hardware, likely set up with the default password.

The perils of an exposed NAS

Open season for attacks

You'll also be horribly wrong to presume your little NAS is too small a target for bad actors. When a port-hunting bot finds an open port to your network, it typically tries to break in using a list of common default usernames and passwords. Once inside, your NAS becomes the doorway to your home network, and attackers can access other connected devices, such as computers, smart TVs, security cameras, and smartphones.

Dedicated search engines such as Shodan.io make short work of finding exposed ports and services by aiding their discoverability. If your services are exposed, they'll likely end up here too. There are even entire directories of security cameras that users have inadvertently left exposed to the internet available on Shodan and other dedicated repositories, which is evidence enough that people are looking for these things, and no breach is too insignificant to bother.

In the worst case, attacks affecting your home Wi-Fi lead to ransomware that encrypts every file you own, like the QNAP QLocker ransomware attack in 2021. It could also lead to theft of your banking information, personal identity, and crypto wallets. They can even use your network devices' processing power to mine cryptocurrency, slowing them to a crawl while you foot the utilities bill.

Sure, some NAS vendors and their software utilities do the legwork of a secure setup for you. You'll be fine with basic sanitation measures, such as secure passwords that are not reused, multi-factor authentication, non-default credentials, and port forwarding. Additionally, consider IP blocking after multiple failed logins and enabling automatic updates. Synology's DSM operating system allows configuring all this securely, but the default QuickConnect setup process doesn't go as far.

Intermediate services like QuickConnect or Plex Pass for remote streaming are generally a better option than direct port forwarding because they often use a third-party relay server. Your NAS connects to their server, and you connect to their server. This avoids punching a direct hole in your firewall. However, if you're using a third-party server to broker the connection, you might as well consider paying directly for a dedicated cloud service. Either way, you're entrusting an intermediary with your data for a fee that ensures your connection is reliable while the data is secure.

Setting up remote access correctly

To avoid remote access

  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  

If you absolutely must have remote access, there are much safer ways to do it. Most users should re-evaluate their needs and invest in portable storage they can carry instead. However, if you still conclude you need remote access, please don't set about opening ports on your router. A secure VPN tunnel to your router is many orders of magnitude more secure. As the name suggests, tunnels are direct connections between two devices on the web with zero open ports at either end. Many businesses prefer this access method, but VPNs are still exposed via a network port that remains susceptible to vulnerabilities and production-level attacks.

Network ports are a lot safer than open router ports because the latter can fall victim to a brute-force attack quickly. Meanwhile, WireGuard connections introduce many more variables that deter intruders.

As such, setting up Tailscale or WireGuard and using those as VPN tunnels is a decent middle ground. Tailscale sets up an outbound tunnel from your NAS to an internet node, which your remote access device also connects to. It's not an involved process for a novice, but in either case, you'll be responsible for creating and managing the security credentials for anyone who needs access. It's the most robust way to keep things locked down.

There's no wrong choice

If setting up user credentials, managing permissions, and getting comfortable with terms in this article sounds like a headache, chances are you're better off without remote access.

No matter if you're using a VPN tunnel to your NAS or a proprietary service like Synology QuickConnect, ports open up to enable these connections, and there's always a non-zero chance a stranger on the internet can break in. This isn't meant to be fear-mongering or gatekeeping. It's a genuine precaution given the nuances of networking and the data at stake. If you're not a networking expert or willing to become one, keep your NAS off the internet, and use a cloud storage service when needed. In resisting the temptation to make it accessible from everywhere, you avoid becoming the low-hanging fruit to automated attacks.

The "waterfall" touchpad lacks a bezel entirely at the top, starting immediately from where the keyboard ends, and spans down almost to the very bottom of the chassis. The size is awesome, but the fact that it's also haptic is very welcome. My only gripe is a rather small nitpick, but it caught me very off-guard. The keyboard itself has excellent travel and feels very at home beneath my fingers. The keys have a satisfying "clack" but aren't harsh to the ears, even if you're rather heavy-fingered like I am.

item.title: I used Poweramp and YouTube Music side by side on Android Auto for a month, and the winner surprised me
item.itunes:title: I used Poweramp and YouTube Music side by side on Android Auto for a month, and the winner surprised me
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Poweramp and YouTube Music take two different approaches to music on Android Auto. One focuses on streaming, recommendations, and convenience, while the other gives me far more control over a local music library.

I wanted to see which approach actually works better once I am behind the wheel, so I used both apps side by side for an entire month. I paid attention to sound quality, offline playback, navigation, library management, and how quickly I could start playing what I wanted without getting distracted.

After weeks of switching between them, one app clearly fits my Android Auto setup better.

Poweramp gives me far more control over sound

YouTube Music wins on pure convenience

This is where Poweramp immediately started pulling ahead for me. It gives me far more control over how my music sounds in the car, with a proper equalizer, presets, bass and treble adjustments, balance controls, and plenty of other options to fine-tune playback. I could actually tweak the sound around my car speakers instead of simply accepting whatever the streaming app gave me. The catch is that Poweramp isn’t plug-and-play.

I first had to build my local library, transfer the music to my phone, organize folders, make sure the metadata was correct, and spend some time dialing in the sound. It takes more effort up front, and you need good, high-quality car speakers to hear all those tiny details.

YouTube Music takes the exact opposite approach, and that is also its biggest strength. I can simply open Android Auto, search for an artist, playlist, or random song, and start listening within seconds. If I suddenly remember a track I haven’t heard in years, chances are it is already there. Compared to Poweramp, it requires almost no setup (except an active monthly subscription).

Poweramp gives me more control, but YouTube Music makes music playback almost effortless.

Offline playback is where Poweramp feels dependable

Poweramp makes a curated local library feel better

Offline playback is where Poweramp has an upper hand. My entire music library is already stored locally, so there is nothing to download before a trip, no connection to worry about, and no chance of a playlist suddenly being unavailable when the network drops.

I can open Poweramp, pick an album, folder, artist, or playlist, and start listening immediately. YouTube Music technically handles offline music well, but getting to it feels more cumbersome on Android Auto. I have to go to More > Downloads, then pick the playlist I want. The UX could have been better. It is not a huge inconvenience, but when I am behind the wheel, those extra steps matter. Once my library was set up, it felt more dependable every time I drove.

Poweramp also made me appreciate having a curated local music library again. Instead of opening an app and being greeted with recommendations, mixes, and whatever an algorithm thinks I should hear next, I look at a collection I built myself.

Once I tagged and arranged everything properly, finding music became quick. YouTube Music is clearly better for endless discovery, but for the music I already know and love, Poweramp makes the connection easier to enjoy.

I changed my Android Auto dashboard, and it instantly became more useful and productive

A smarter layout for every drive.

By  Parth Shah

Voice control gives YouTube Music an edge

Poweramp isn’t far behind

I expected YouTube Music to beat Poweramp on voice controls. With Gemini on Android Auto, I can ask for a specific song, playlist, or artist without touching the screen. I can even be more descriptive, such as mentioning a scene, an artist, and the movie it appeared in, and Gemini can usually figure out what I am trying to play. That kind of flexibility is a major advantage when I am driving.

But Poweramp surprised me. I asked Gemini to play a specific song using Poweramp, and it worked like a charm. I only need to remember the track name.

Poweramp can’t match all the fancy discovery and contextual requests that YouTube Music supports, but I don’t need it to. Being able to request a specific song from my local library with a basic Gemini command covers one of my biggest concerns about switching.

Although this comparison is about Android Auto, I also want to talk about their mobile apps.

Poweramp is a joy to use with a clean UI and thoughtful animations. YouTube Music isn’t far behind, but it surely felt busy with too many recommendations and album art. Poweramp also offers a lifetime plan, so I can buy the app once and use it on all my devices.

The better player wasn’t surprising

After a month of using both on Android Auto, Poweramp is the one staying in my setup. YouTube Music is still the easier app to recommend if you just want instant access and seamless voice commands. But for the way I actually listen in the car, Poweramp fits better. It sounds better, handles offline playback like a pro, and even works with Gemini for basic commands.

Poweramp
See at Google Play Store

Offline playback is where Poweramp has an upper hand. My entire music library is already stored locally, so there is nothing to download before a trip, no connection to worry about, and no chance of a playlist suddenly being unavailable when the network drops.

I changed my Android Auto dashboard, and it instantly became more useful and productive

A smarter layout for every drive.

I expected YouTube Music to beat Poweramp on voice controls. With Gemini on Android Auto, I can ask for a specific song, playlist, or artist without touching the screen. item.title: Wi-Fi 8 is the first wireless upgrade in years that isn't chasing speed, and home networks need it
item.itunes:title: Wi-Fi 8 is the first wireless upgrade in years that isn't chasing speed, and home networks need it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You could easily spend hundreds of dollars on a high-end tri-band Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 mesh system. The box will promise you blanket multi-gigabit coverage across a 5,000-square-foot home; however, the real-world experience is plagued by weird and erratic wireless behavior. Your phone might desperately cling to a distant node instead of handing off cleanly, and download speeds in your office might spike, causing jitter and packet loss for someone gaming in the living room.

This is because mesh nodes aren't truly unified radios. They are independent access points that effectively fight each other for airtime, step over each other's channel allocations, and can create self-inflicted co-channel interference. The biggest bottleneck in your home network probably isn't raw speed. It's the chaotic lack of coordination between multiple access points operating on the same spectrum. Wi-Fi 8's killer feature, multi-AP coordination (otherwise known as MAPC), transforms isolated mesh satellites from competing radio silos into a synchronized microsecond-level phased antenna array.

5 reasons I’d always choose mesh Wi-Fi over a traditional router

When it comes to routers, I’d choose a mesh router every time. Here’s why.

12
By  Cierra Noffke

A mesh network might not be the solution

There are a range of problems

Current mesh networks are essentially broken due to limitations. Wi-Fi still relies on carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance. This means that before an access point or client transmits, it must listen to the medium. That means if node B, which is in the living room, detects energy from node A, which is in the office, on the same or overlapping channel, it backs off and waits. Your mesh nodes actively throttle each other's transmission opportunities.

There's also the sticky client dilemma. Current fast-roaming standards only suggest transitions to the client, but your smartphone or laptop makes the final roaming decision. This sometimes will lead to a device hanging onto a -78 dBm weak signal from the bedroom node rather than roaming to the -45 dBm node 2 feet away, ruining airtime efficiency for the entire BSSID.

Even if you have dedicated 6GHz backhaul, uncoordinated spatial streams can create radio frequency reflection multipath interference, causing dropped frames and sudden retransmission spikes.

Wi-Fi 8 might solve all of these problems

Thanks to some new architecture

So what changes when it comes to Wi-Fi 8? Well, it technically has a secret weapon in the form of multi-AP coordination, sometimes called MAPC. These core architectural pillars redefine mesh topology.

You get coordinated beamforming. In current mesh setups, when two nodes transmit simultaneously, their side lobes cause mutual interference, but with coordinated beamforming, node A and node B can exchange channel state information and mathematically shape their nulls. Node A, for example, can direct RF energy strictly at your laptop while actively placing a spatial null in the physical direction of node B's active clients.

There's also coordinated spatial reuse. Instead of Node B falling silent when it hears Node A transmitting, the coordinating primary AP dynamically dictates transmit power limits via a coordinated spatial reuse frame. Node B will calculate that Node A is transmitting to a client on the far left, meaning it will safely transmit to its nearby kitchen client at 12 dBm without raising the noise floor on Node A's link. Simultaneous transmissions occur cleanly without packet collisions.

You also get seamless roaming and deterministic handoffs. Moving handoff negotiation from client-driven polling to access-point-orchestrated handshakes means that you're reducing handoff frame drops and latency spikes in theory.

And lastly, dynamic sub-channel operation as well as non-primary channel access. This prevents a single narrowband IoT sensor or slow client from locking up an entire 160 MHz or 320 MHz wide block of spectrum.

Should you upgrade now?

Wait for Wi-Fi 8 or stick to 7?

So when it comes to upgrading, what should you actually do? Should you buy Wi-Fi 7 now or wait for Wi-Fi 8?

Right now, when it comes to the timeline for Wi-Fi 8, draft specifications and early silicon demonstrations are hitting the pipeline. Certified consumer hardware and final IEEE 802.11be ratification will land around 2027 or 2028, so there's still a little bit of a waiting game here.

There's also the issue of the client upgrade stumbling block. MAPC requires both access point coordination and client-side understanding of new control frames to unlock its potential, so your 2024 smartphone won't magically become a seamless roaming node overnight, unfortunately.

What does this mean? If your current setup is suffering from dead zones today, you'd probably benefit from buying a reputable wired backhaul or Wi-Fi 6 or 6E on sale, or even a stable Wi-Fi 7 router. However, if you're holding out for an expensive multi-node flagship wireless mesh because you want rock-solid zero-jitter gaming and stutter-free roaming, then Wi-Fi 8 is the generation worth waiting for. Keep in mind that you might be waiting a while.

Speeds aren't everything

Wi-Fi 8 is so much more than that

For 20 years, the Wi-Fi Alliance sold us bigger throughput numbers that almost no residential application could actually saturate. We didn't need 40 Gbps to stream 4K video or play online games. We needed a network that didn't drop packets when we walked down the hallway.

Wi-Fi 8 represents the moment wireless networking finally grew up. By prioritizing reliability over speed vanity metrics, it promises to turn mesh networking from a marketing compromise into the seamless invisible utility it should have been from the start.
